o: We need to check whether the element at index n/2 (the middle of an odd-length array) occurs exactly once in the whole array. For [1,2,3], the middle is 2 and it appears once, so the answer is true. For [1,2,2], the middle is 2 but it appears twice, so the answer is false. With n ≤ 100 and values ≤ 100, even a brute-force double loop is trivially fast; a counting approach gives O(n) time.
k: The middle element of an odd-length array of length n is at index n/2 (integer division).
Counting occurrences with a hash map or frequency array lets us answer in one pass plus a lookup.
With tiny constraints (n ≤ 100), any correct approach works; prefer the simplest readable solution.

a.i: Find the middle value at index n/2, then scan the entire array counting how many times it appears. If the count equals 1, return true. This directly mirrors the problem statement and needs no extra data structures.
s: Initialize count = 0 and iterate over every element of nums.
Increment count whenever an element equals mid.
Return true if count == 1, otherwise false.
a.t: O(n) — two linear scans over the array (one pass suffices since we capture mid first).
a.sp: O(1) — only a counter is stored.

a.i: Since values are bounded by 100, build a frequency table in one pass, then check whether freq[nums[n/2]] == 1. This generalizes naturally if you later need counts of many elements or repeated queries.
s: Create a frequency map (or int array of size 101 for C++/Java).
Iterate through nums once, incrementing the frequency of each value.
Look up the frequency of nums[n / 2].
Return true iff that frequency is exactly 1.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build frequencies plus an O(1) lookup.
a.sp: O(n) for a hash map (or O(1) effectively, using a fixed-size array of 101 slots given bounded values).

w: In an interview, the brute-force count is perfectly acceptable here given the constraints; mention the frequency-array variant as a natural generalization when multiple queries on counts are needed. Pitfalls: remember the middle index is n/2 with integer division only because n is odd; don't forget the middle element itself contributes to its own count (so count must be exactly 1, not 0 elsewhere). Edge cases: n = 1 always returns true since the single middle element appears once. Follow-ups might ask for the answer after point updates (use a frequency map with incremental updates) or for all elements appearing exactly once.
